Now let me compile a comprehensive verse-by-verse commentary from the sources I've accessed.

## Ezekiel 47 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter has two main sections: **vv. 1–12** — the vision of the life-giving river flowing from the temple; **vv. 13–23** — the boundaries and distribution of the land among the twelve tribes. Ellicott calls vv. 1–12 "the vision of the living waters" and notes that vv. 13–23 properly belong with ch. 48. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)

Gill introduces the chapter as an account of "the vision of the holy waters" and "the borders of the holy land, and the division of it to Israelites and strangers." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)

---

### vv. 1–2 — The River's Source: The Temple

**v. 1:** The man (the angelic guide of Ezekiel 40:3) brings Ezekiel back to the door of the temple. Water flows from under the threshold eastward, coming from the south (right) side of the temple, south of the altar.

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** The river originates from God's house, not a palace, government building, or marketplace. "Significantly, the river does not come from a king's palace or a government building… It comes from God's house." Jerusalem never had such a river historically; in the semi-arid geography, a river like this was both a blessing and a miracle. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **Gill:** The waters issue from the holy of holies — the seat of the divine Majesty and throne of God. He notes the Talmudists say the fountain came first from the house of the holy of holies, under its threshold. Gill applies it figuratively to the Gospel: "this is not of men, but God; comes from heaven, the holy of holies; and out of the house and church of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)
- **Ellicott:** "Door of the house" means the entrance of the Temple itself. The waters come from under its threshold, just as in Revelation 22:1 they proceed "out of the throne of God and of the Lamb." The waters had to deflect southward to pass the porch and altar. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Bible.org (Utley):** "For desert people water was a sign of God's blessing and presence (i.e., Joel 3:18). The eschatological sense is present in Zech. 13:1 and 14:8. It is used by John in Rev. 22:1, 17." He calls it "metaphorical (cf. Ps. 46:4; 65:9) and not meant to be taken literally." (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-47)

**v. 2:** Ezekiel is led out through the north gate, around the outside, to the outer east gate, where he sees water trickling from the south side.

- **Ellicott:** The east gate was shut (Ezekiel 44:2), so the prophet was carried round to the outside of it via the north gate. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Gill:** The Hebrew word for "ran out" (מְפַכִּים) means water flowing "like water out of the mouth of a vial" — very small, still, and easy. The rabbi Bartenora says the prophet first saw the waters "come out very small, like the horns of a locust." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)
- **Guzik:** Notes Clarke's comment: "The waters seem to have been at first in small quantity; for the words imply that they oozed or dropped out. They were at first so small that they came, drop by drop; but they increased." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)

---

### vv. 3–6 — The River's Increasing Depth

**v. 3:** The guide measures 1,000 cubits eastward; water is ankle-deep.

- **Gill:** This first measuring may signify "the ministry of John the Baptist" or "the more easy doctrines of the Gospel; those waters which Christ's lambs may wade in; that milk which new born babes desire … such as salvation by Christ alone; justification by his righteousness; peace and pardon by his blood." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)
- **Ellicott:** The measuring point is assumed to be from the threshold (the source). Ezekiel is made to pass through the waters at each stage to impress upon him a vivid sense of their depth. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Guzik:** Notes the LXX mistranslated "water of ankles" as "water of remission," leading early Christian commentators to apply this to baptism — "A warning to both translators and interpreters!" (quoting Taylor). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)

**v. 4:** Two more measurements of 1,000 cubits each: knee-deep, then waist-deep.

- **Gill:** Waters to the knees and loins may signify "the greater knowledge of the Gospel, and the mysteries of it, the apostles had after the Spirit was poured forth … or else those doctrines … which are more sublime, and more difficult to understand; as concerning predestination, election, the covenant of grace … which are meat for strong men." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)
- **Guzik:** The rapid increase in depth — from a trickle to waist-deep in about a mile — is miraculous. "We read nothing of other streams leading into this; it is a miraculous and abundant provision." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)

**v. 5:** A fourth 1,000 cubits; now an uncrossable river deep enough for swimming.

- **Ellicott:** The whole distance is 4,000 cubits (less than 1½ miles), during which waters "without external addition, have swollen from a mere streamlet to an impassable river, in direct opposition to the ordinary fact in nature." This illustrates "the increase of the kingdom of God — the same truth illustrated by our Lord in the parable of the mustard seed (Matthew 13:31-32)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Gill:** The fourth measuring may refer to "the latter day glory." This depth signifies "some doctrines exceeding deep, out of the reach and penetration of men, called the deep things of God … such as the trinity of Persons in the Godhead … the generation of the Son; the procession of the Spirit; the incarnation of Christ; the union of the two natures in his person; the resurrection of the dead, &c." These are only reached "in the swimming arms of faith." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)
- **Guzik (citing Spurgeon):** Spurgeon saw a spiritual analogy between the life of faith and swimming. We start "floating in faith," then progress to swimming by faith. "How blessedly our friend Mr. Mueller of Bristol swims! … He has had his feet off the bottom many years." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **Guzik (citing Trapp):** Many have seen the deepening water as an illustration of the depths of Scripture: "Scriptures have their shallows wherein the lamb may wade, like as they have their profundities wherein the elephant himself may swim." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **F.B. Meyer (cited at Precept Austin):** "We need the ankle-depths of walking to be exchanged for the knee-depths of praying; and these for the loin-depths of perfect purity; and these for the length, depth, breadth, and height of the love of Christ." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-f_b_meyer)

**v. 6:** "Son of man, do you see this?" Then Ezekiel is led back to the riverbank.

- **Gill:** The guide asks, "hast thou carefully observed all this from whence the waters flowed? from what small beginnings they rose, and gradually increased?" It is "right and profitable to observe the rise and progress of the Gospel." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)
- **Ellicott:** The angel calls the prophet's attention to the marvellous increase, then causes him to return along the bank to observe other things. "The prophet does not return to the brink, for he had not left it, but is told to pass along it." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)

---

### vv. 7–12 — The Power of the River

**v. 7:** A great number of trees along both banks.

- **Gill:** "Here was a new wonder observed … on a sudden sprung up trees on each side of the river, of a perfect stature, and full of fruit." An emblem of true Christians — "trees of righteousness, planted by the river of divine love; watered with the grace of God, and doctrines of the Gospel." Notes the Hebrew can be read as "an exceeding large tree" (cf. Revelation 22:2's singular "tree of life"). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)
- **Ellicott:** The "very many trees" correspond symbolically to the "tree of life, which bare twelve manner of fruits" in Revelation 22:2. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)

**v. 8:** The water flows east to the Arabah and into the Dead Sea, making its waters fresh.

- **Ellicott:** "The word for country is the same as is used in Joshua 22:10-11, for the borders of the Jordan … the valley of the Jordan, called the Ghor." The "desert" is better translated "plain" — the expansion of the Jordan valley just north of the Dead Sea near Jericho. "Both the situation and the description show that the Dead Sea is intended." The waters "shall be healed" means changed from being incapable of supporting life to becoming a home of life. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Guzik:** "There is also an obvious but possibly overlooked point here: God cares about the environment and promises to restore and heal it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **Guzik (citing Block):** "'Its waters are miraculously healed,' rapa normally refers to the healing of a diseased body, but in this case the miracle involves neutralizing the baneful chemicals in the water, so it becomes fresh." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **Gill:** The Gospel was first preached in the eastern parts; it "went down into the desert" (the Gentile world, formerly a desert) and "into the sea" (the Dead Sea, emblem of dead sinners). "The waters shall be healed" means "the change made in sinful men by means of the Gospel, who are thereby quickened." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)
- **Bible.org (Utley):** "Many commentators have asserted that the verse refers to a miraculous change of saltwater to fresh water, but it seems to me that it refers to the abundance of waters which fills up the Arabah depression and overflows it." (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-47)

**v. 9:** Swarms of living creatures, a great number of fish; wherever the river flows, everything flourishes.

- **Ellicott:** The Hebrew word for "rivers" is pointed as a dual ("two rivers"), causing perplexity. Zechariah 14:8 has waters divided between Dead Sea and Mediterranean. But here "but one river is intended … the dual form is simply used to express the greatness of the river, 'a double river.'" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Gill:** "Everything that liveth, which moveth" refers to "every living man … whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live" — spiritually. "To all to whom it is accompanied by the Spirit of God it is the savour of life unto life." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)
- **Spurgeon (via Precept Austin):** "The living waters, in the prophet's vision, flowed into the Dead Sea and carried life with them, even into that stagnant lake. Where grace goes, spiritual life is the immediate and the everlasting consequence. Grace proceeds sovereignly according to the will of God, even as a river in all its windings follows its own sweet will." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_ezekiel)
- **Sermon Bible Commentary (via StudyLight):** The river pictures the gift of the Holy Spirit: (1) to the patriarchs; (2) to pious Israelites and prophets; (3) during Christ's ministry; (4) on the Day of Pentecost. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/sbc/ezekiel-47.html)

**v. 10:** Fishermen stand from En-gedi to En-eglaim spreading nets; fish of many kinds like the Great Sea.

- **Ellicott:** En-gedi is "a well-known copious spring about midway on the western coast of the Dead Sea." En-eglaim occurs only here. Jerome placed it at the junction of the Jordan with the sea. The dual form may indicate "one of the double cities of Moab" on the eastern side. "Everywhere they shall stretch their nets, and the variety and abundance of the fish shall be as great as in 'the great sea,' that is, the Mediterranean." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Gill:** The "fishers" are "the apostles of Christ, who, of fishermen, were made fishers of men … and so were the instruments of saving them, even of great numbers, both in Judea, and in the Gentile world." Also "all other ministers of the Gospel … especially those that will be in the latter day." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)
- **Guzik:** Jesus may have had this image in mind when He spoke of rivers of living water (John 7:37-38). "There is a valid spiritual application of this wonderful image, and a literal fulfillment to come." However, he notes that Trapp spiritualized it entirely: "These fishers are Christ's apostles and ministers, who are called fishers of men." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)

**v. 11:** The swamps and marshes will not become fresh; they will be left for salt.

- **Ellicott:** "The picture of the life-giving waters would be imperfect without this exception to their effects." The Dead Sea's southern end is very shallow, and beyond it low land is overflowed seasonally, then left bare and encrusted with salt. This shows that "the effect of the life-giving waters should cease where the waters themselves ceased to flow." Symbolically, "it shows that we are not to expect, as the effect of the Gospel, a perfect and universal obedience to its teachings. Man is still left free to hear or forbear, and the world must be expected always to contain its unhealed miry and marshy places." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Guzik (citing Block):** "The preservation of some pockets of saltiness is intentional, recognizing the economic benefit of the minerals found in and around the Dead Sea. Salt (melah) is not only a valuable seasoning and preserving agent; the word functions generically for a wide range of chemicals extracted from the sea." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **Gill:** Those who reject the Gospel are not healed — "to some it is not profitable … but is the savour of death unto death." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)
- **Guzik also notes Clarke's anti-Catholic interpretation:** Clarke thought the swamps pictured "the Roman Catholic Church, that is both schismatic and heretic from the Church of Jesus Christ." Guzik presents this as an example of "overly-spiritualized" reading. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)

**v. 12:** Fruit trees of all kinds along both banks; leaves never wither, fruit never fails, bearing each month. Fruit for food, leaves for healing.

- **Pulpit Commentary (via BibleHub):** The trees' productivity is due not merely to moisture but to the fact that "the waters which they drank up issued out of the sanctuary." The picture "is unmistakably based on Genesis 2:9, and is as clearly reproduced by the Apocalyptic seer in Revelation 22:2." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/47-12.htm)
- **Ellicott:** "These trees with their supernatural virtues are represented as produced by the waters because 'they issued out of the sanctuary,' thus presenting a most effective image of the life-giving power of those spiritual influences which come from God upon men." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Gill:** The fruit trees represent "true Christians, believers, and regenerate persons, who are trees of righteousness … whereby they become fruitful in good works." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)

---

### vv. 13–14 — The Promise of the Land; Two Portions for Joseph

**v. 13:** The Lord GOD declares the boundaries; the land divided among the twelve tribes; Joseph receives two portions.

- **Guzik:** "This emphasizes that this was not a symbolic or spiritual land; God gave specific borders to mark it. There will be real land that will be given to the real twelve tribes of Israel." Joseph's two portions = Ephraim and Manasseh, as under Joshua. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **Ellicott:** In the ideal land, not just Judah and Benjamin but all twelve tribes receive portions. Levi is provided for in the "oblation," so Joseph receives two portions (per Genesis 48:5, 22). The Hebrew is simply "Joseph portions" in the plural. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Guzik (citing Block):** "'Although the nation had been divided politically for nearly four hundred years, as in the case of all his prophetic colleagues Ezekiel's vision of Israel's future is based on the tradition of a united nation consisting of twelve tribes of Israel descended from Jacob's twelve sons.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)

**v. 14:** Divided equally; God swore with uplifted hand to give it to the forefathers.

- **Ellicott:** "Unlike the former division of the land, the territory is to be arranged in twelve equal portions." However, he notes that since the country was nearly three times as broad at the south as at the north, the actual area would vary considerably even if strips were of equal width. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)

---

### vv. 15–20 — The Borders of the Land

**v. 15–17 (Northern border):** From the Great Sea via Hethlon through Lebo-hamath to Zedad, Berothah, Sibraim (between Damascus and Hamath), as far as Hazer-hatticon (border of Hauran), then to Hazar-enan.

- **Ellicott:** The boundaries are "essentially the same as those given in Numbers 34:1-15, only that there the southern boundary is given first … while here the northern is first described for the people supposed to be returning from Babylon." The eastern boundary notably is still the Jordan — the trans-Jordanian tribal territories are excluded. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Guzik:** "Only twice in Israel's history did the political borders of Israel extend as far north as Lebo-hamath: under David and under Jeroboam II." He notes Daniel Block's map would include all of Lebanon and a good portion of Syria (including Damascus) but not modern Jordan or Egypt. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **Bible.org (Utley):** The southern boundaries are close to Joshua's boundaries and the kingdoms of David and Solomon, "but the northern part is expanded northward and eastward as far as Hamath and including most of Syria." (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-47)

**v. 18 (Eastern border):** Between Hauran and Damascus, along the Jordan between Gilead and Israel, to the Eastern Sea as far as Tamar.

- **Ellicott:** The word "from" is literally "from between" — the boundary runs between Hauran, Damascus, Gilead on one side and Israel on the other. The boundary is the Jordan; but since the Jordan does not extend so far north, Damascus territory bounds Israel. The boundary extends beyond the mouth of the Jordan to the southern end of the Dead Sea and Kadesh. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)

**v. 19 (Southern border):** From Tamar to the waters of Meribath-kadesh, along the Brook of Egypt to the Great Sea.

- **Ellicott:** Tamar has been identified with Kurnub (a ruined village west of the southern Dead Sea), but since Kadesh is about 30 miles south of the Dead Sea, "the Tamar here meant is more probably some place not yet identified." Kadesh = Kadesh-barnea (Numbers 34:4). "The river" = the Wady-el-Arish (Rhinocolura). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)

**v. 20 (Western border):** The Great Sea up to a point opposite Lebo-hamath.

- **Guzik:** The western boundary is the Mediterranean. He notes (citing Alexander): "In contrast the land of God's people in the eternal state will have no sea since the sea will no longer exist (Revelation 21:1)." This shows Ezekiel's vision is of the millennial kingdom, not the eternal state. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)

---

### vv. 21–23 — Division Among the Tribes; Inclusion of Foreigners

**v. 21:** The land divided among the tribes of Israel.

- **Guzik:** "The repeated commands to divide the land indicate that this is a real land, not a spiritual representation. The best way to understand this is that this division of the land is yet to come, but will come in a kingdom period when the world is ruled in a direct way by Jesus Messiah." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)

**v. 22:** Foreigners who dwell among Israel and have children are to be treated as native-born; they receive an inheritance among the tribes.

- **Ellicott:** "An entirely new feature is here added to the Mosaic law. According to Leviticus 19:34, strangers were to be treated with kindness, but the entire territory was to be divided among the Israelites, and strangers could therefore acquire no land except in so far as they might purchase a temporary right between the years of Jubilee. Now, however, such of them as 'shall beget children among you,' thus showing a disposition to permanent residence, are to receive an inheritance along with the tribes … This privilege is absolute, without any condition of receiving circumcision." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Guzik (citing Vawter and Hoppe):** "'The Pentateuch prescribes humane treatment for the aliens living in Israel (cf. Exodus 22:21; 23:9; Leviticus 19:10, 33-34; 23:22; Deuteronomy 14:29; 24:14-15, 17-22). … Ezekiel goes far beyond the Torah's legislation.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **Guzik (citing Taylor):** "It is based on the principle that if these men choose to accept the standards, the religion and the way of life within Israel as a permanency, i.e. as proselytes who settle and have children there (Ezekiel 47:22), then they are entitled to the same treatment as native Israelites." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **Bible.org (Utley):** "This is the one section of the book that seems to be inclusive instead of exclusive. This is similar to Isa. 56:3-8 and follows the pattern of Lev. 24:22 and Num. 15:29." (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-47)

**v. 23:** In whatever tribe a foreigner dwells, his inheritance is assigned there.

---

## Key Tradition-Specific Differences

### Literal vs. Symbolic/Spiritual Interpretation of the River

This is the major divide among Protestant traditions regarding Ezekiel 47:

**Dispensational Premillennial (Literal future kingdom):**
- **David Guzik / Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Insists the river, trees, healed Dead Sea, and land boundaries are "real" — "a real river in a real Messianic kingdom to come." Yet he simultaneously draws spiritual analogies (going deeper in faith). The river "can and will be fulfilled both literally in a coming kingdom age and is also a fitting symbol of God's present work through the gospel." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **John MacArthur / GTY:** In a sermon on "The Coming Earthly Kingdom of the Lord Jesus Christ," MacArthur cites Ezekiel 47's fish in the Dead Sea as a literal future transformation. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/66-74/the-coming-earthly-kingdom-of-the-lord-jesus-christ-part-2)
- **Dr. Constable's Expository Notes (Dallas Theological Seminary):** "The river that Ezekiel saw was a real river with life-giving and healing properties. But like the rivers in Genesis 2 and Revelation 22 it also has symbolic significance. Many interpreters spiritualize the entire passage and see no literal fulfillment in the future." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-47.html — cited in search results)
- **Precept Austin:** Self-identifies as adhering to "a literal interpretation of the Scriptures, a belief that God is not yet finished with the nation of Israel, a belief in a literal return of Christ to literally reign and rule on the earth for 1000 years." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_commentaries)

**Amillennial / Covenant / Spiritual (Primarily symbolic):**
- **Gill (Reformed Baptist, 18th century):** Treats the entire vision as figurative of the Gospel and its effects throughout church history. The waters are "the Gospel, and the doctrines of it"; the Dead Sea represents "dead sinners"; the fishermen are "the apostles of Christ." No expectation of a literal future river. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-47.html)
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** States plainly: "The ideal character of this vision of the waters is so plain upon its face that little need be said on this point." He sees water as "the symbol of the influence of the Spirit." He explicitly rejects literal interpretation: "if the whole were to be literally understood, they [fishermen] would really have no place, because there would be no such fishermen in the supposed glorified condition of the land." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary Homiletics:** The river is "the river of the gospel of Christ … the river of Divine truth." All four depth stages picture the growth of the kingdom through church history. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Bible.org (Utley):** States the water is "metaphorical (cf. Ps. 46:4; 65:9) and not meant to be taken literally." Conveys "original creation, Eden, covenant promises." (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-47)

### The Swamps and Marshes (v. 11)

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Teaches that the unhealed marshes demonstrate "we are not to expect, as the effect of the Gospel, a perfect and universal obedience to its teachings. Man is still left free to hear or forbear." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Block (cited by Guzik):** Sees a positive economic purpose: salt and minerals remain available for human use. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **Clarke (cited by Guzik, older Methodist):** Applied it polemically to the Roman Catholic Church — a reading Guzik labels "overly-spiritualized." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)

### Inclusion of Foreigners (v. 22)

- **Ellicott:** Notes this goes "far beyond the Torah's legislation" and is granted "without any condition of receiving circumcision." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Guzik:** Sees this as part of the inclusive justice of the coming millennial kingdom — strangers who choose to dwell in Israel under Messiah's rule receive full inheritance rights. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)
- **Bible.org (Utley):** Highlights this as "the one section of the book that seems to be inclusive instead of exclusive," paralleling Isaiah 56:3-8. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-47)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic Emphasis

- **David Guzik (Enduring Word):** While holding to literal future fulfillment, strongly emphasizes the experiential call to "go deeper" — "God's people read this and feel a call to go deeper. They shouldn't stop until they are swimming, carried along by God's currents and comfortable in that place." The river is something "to enter into," not just observe. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-47/)

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes, via Ellicott's reference)

- The dual form of "rivers" (נַחֲלַיִם) in v. 9 has generated scholarly discussion. Ellicott notes some scholars propose a slight vowel change would yield "river of the sea." The dual may simply express greatness — "a double river." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/47.htm)
- **Peake's Commentary (modernist, early 20th century):** Treats the vision as "splendid imagination" that "vividly suggests the beneficent and life-giving influences that will stream forth from the Church of God upon the sick and famished souls of a dead and arid world." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-47.html)

### Catholic and Orthodox Views

- No pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org dealing directly with Ezekiel 47 appeared in searches. The search tool was limited to the sites that came up. From what was found, the **older patristic reading** (referenced by Gill and Guzik) saw the waters as baptism (the LXX "water of remission" mistranslation) and the river as the Church's sacramental life flowing to the world.

### Word of Faith / Prosperity Teaching

- No direct pages from prosperity or Word of Faith teachers were retrieved in these searches. However, Guzik's emphasis on the river as something believers must actively "enter into" for healing and abundance, and his framing of the trees' leaves as "medicine," could be noted as themes that some prosperity teachers have drawn upon — though Guzik himself anchors his teaching in a literal future kingdom.
